summary: Round 5, scoped to my round-3 findings (tr-16..tr-19). All four are fixed and I verified each against the code rather than against the prose. tr-16: CONFIRMED and I agree with the new prescription. LocalSequencer.start:228-239 calls recoverChainEnd on the inheritable ancestor and then seal(), whose Seal lands at keyFor(seq) = '<16 hex>.delta' -- which sorts before 'ckpt/' -- so the later crossing (start:255 -> open -> ChainReplay.inherited -> applyChain) returns at that Seal (ChainReplay.java:336-341) and never reaches a ckpt key. The takeover destroys applyChain's fixture by construction, exactly as the row now states. Driving the two calls directly against one unsealed checkpoint-bearing chain is STRICTLY STRONGER than my own round-3 suggestion of a plain takeover with a seeded predecessor: replayAncestry adds hops[0]=(epoch, MAX_VALUE) unconditionally (ChainReplay.java:139), so recover() over a chain whose slot 0 is a CommitDelta (CommitLogTest:415-421's fixture shape) walks no ancestry and reaches applyChain with the whole key set; recoverChainEnd() takes the LAST key (ChainReplay.java:96-113) which is the ckpt key and GETs it, so it throws pre-fix. Two independent red tests, two independent failures -- whereas in the takeover shape both sites surface identically as 'start released the lease', and post-chainEnd-fix the applyChain site is unreachable. tr-17: the split is correct -- the interposed '<seq>.delta.tmp' with a non-decodable body kills the deny-list and contains() predicates at BOTH sites (each makes the tmp key be read and decode-fail), and the added offsets/nextSequence assertion is what kills return-instead-of-continue at applyChain. tr-18: asserting the body's sequence against the key's does kill a constant Checkpoint.sequence with correct keys, and it is the derivation the conditional key criterion cannot reach. tr-19: 'oldestRetainedOffset IS ZERO for every stream' kills StreamOffsets(next, next) and (next, next-1) on any stream with next>0 -- which the neighbouring 'a workload where they differ' clause guarantees -- and cannot misfire at offset 0, because a correct writer emits (0,0) there and 0 == 0. The cap argument's account of my four failure modes is accurate: I re-derived the third mode's mechanism (start seals between the two calls) and the fourth's two halves ((next, next-1) admitted; offset-0 false failure) from the code, and both hold. Two minors, both recorded rather than fixed -- neither admits a production defect against today's key grammar.

findings.summary: The chainEnd site now has a fixture but still no stated ASSERTION beyond 'it must not throw'. The seeding clause's remedy -- 'assert the recovered offsets and nextSequence match the same chain with no interposed key' -- sits inside the applyChain sentence and names 'recovered offsets', which chainEnd deliberately leaves empty (ChainReplay.java:110-112, 'the returned offsets are EMPTY on purpose'), so an implementer reading it as an applyChain-only remedy is reading it plausibly. Apply the same nextSequence assertion to the recoverChainEnd test explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: SURVIVING MUTATION at ChainReplay.java:100-102: implement the chainEnd filter as a stop rather than a skip -- 'for (ObjectStat stat : page.objects()) { if (!stat.key().endsWith(".delta")) break; lastKey = stat.key(); }' -- which is the tempting shape precisely because the row itself argues ckpt sorts last. Against the prescribed shared fixture (deltas 0..N, an interposed <seq>.delta.tmp after delta j, ckpt keys at the end) recoverChainEnd() does not throw and the deny-list/contains mutants are still killed, so a test asserting only 'no longer throws' is green while nextSequence is j+1 instead of N+1 -- a taking-over leader would then seal the predecessor at an already-occupied slot. HONESTLY BOUNDED: against today's key grammar (deltas, then ckpt/) the break form is CORRECT, so this is latent fragility rather than a shipped defect, which is why it is minor and not major -- the same bound applies to the applyChain return/continue mutant the row already covers, and covering one without the other is the inconsistency.
findings.remedy: One clause on the chainEnd sentence: assert nextSequence (and seal) from recoverChainEnd() equals the value the same chain yields with no interposed key.

findings.summary: The rounds:M4.8b entry carries two hand-counted round facts that its own sentence says go stale, and both are now stale in the bytes being committed. '.harness records 25 findings, 12 of them major or blocking' is present tense and false: .harness/review holds 31 findings for M4.8b, 14 major. I reconstructed why -- 25/12 was exactly true after round 2 (a0a6d968: 16, 47aca694: 9) and round 3 (8c78763b: 6, of which 2 major) plus round 4 made it 31/14. The same sentence's remedy, 'named rather than counted', is the fix it declines to take for itself. Second: 'round 2 returned two majors and both were defects in round 1's fixes' under-states the very pattern the entry documents -- round 3 returned a major (tr-16) that was a defect in ROUND 2's fix, which is the entry's own third failure mode.
findings.failure_scenario: A session reading baselines/review.txt for the M4.8b history -- which is the audience the entry names, sessions that have only .harness -- reads 25/12 as a checkable fact, checks it against .harness, finds 31/14, and now distrusts the entry's other numbers, including the ones that are load-bearing. This is the non-negotiable-4 shape in the one file whose worth is that its entries are checkable, and it will be false again the moment this round's verdict is recorded, which is the argument for deleting the count rather than correcting it.
findings.remedy: Delete the two counts, keeping 'it said fifteen across two rounds, which was wrong and is why this entry names rather than counts', and say 'later rounds returned further majors, each a defect in the previous round's fix' without a round number. Recording this in the commit body is also acceptable -- but the stale number is IN the file, so correcting it there is the cheaper of the two.
